I didn't grow up around guns and don't know many gun owners myself. I recently got an M&P Shield 2 and will probably get some more guns in the future. I was just watching a few videos on gun maintenance and wondered if you guys had any tips. Specifically, what cleaner and lube should I use? Is there much difference between the brands or does any one work just fine?
Maintenance tips for an inexperienced owner.

The most pertinent lesson that I learned is not to use the wonder-greases like Slide Glide. At first it feels amazing, but with time they dry up and congeal into a solid substance. For (most) handguns, a tiniest amount of Hoppes #9 is all it takes, unless specified otherwise in the manual.

Buy yourself a 22 rifle (even a pistol too for cheap practice if you like). I wipe down the OUTSIDE of all my guns after I bring them home with a clean rag (or VERY lightly oiled and I stay off the wood/grips). I own a lot of old (though not valuable) stuff so it can be more prone to rust.

I like frog lube. Its It's a bit expensive but some guy did a test where he sprayed salt water on bare steel treated with various lubes and it came out pretty much on top. Also he compared friction reduction with sliding weight at a fixed angle and it did pretty well. You can watch videos about how it's applied but basically you use frog lube solvent to degrease the gun, then you apply the lube, heat with a hair dryer so it absorbs to the metal surface, and WIPE COMPLETELY DRY. If you don't wipe it all off it will congeal and cause problems but it's not a big deal. Just remember, it's a DRY lube which helps avoid dust collection. I used frog lube to get a finiky 1911 100% and it made a gun start locking the slide back on an empty mag when regular clp didn't. Also boresnakes are available pretty cheap from ebay and they are soo much better than patches for a variety of reasons. For one, metal rods can screw your rifling up if used wrong and pulling a boresnake is 100 times faster.
Go to the hardware store and go to the wood cleaning section usually near super glue. They have small brushes there. Get nylon and brass brushes. You can also get a big bag of terry cloth rags.

Back in the old days, people used to clean guns very carefully. In these crazy modern times, changes in ammunition and in the guns themselves have made careful cleaning much less essential.

For a modern pistol like your M&P, the following procedure is fine:

1) Never clean the inside of the barrel. Scrub the chamber with a chamber brush every few hundred rounds and that's it.

2) Wipe the breech face clean, paying particular attention to the space under the extractor. It does not have to be perfect, you just don't want a wad of gunk in there.

3) With a lightly oiled rag, wipe the bulk of the gunk off all the big parts.

4) Lubricate the gun as specified in the manual, and that's it.

In practice, this means that most of the time you just wipe the outside of the gun down after shooting, and wipe the breech face. Add a drop or two of oil to the slide rails and that's it. Literally a minute.

Every now and again - say, every 500 rounds or so - field strip it, scrub the chamber, wipe all the big parts. That's really all it needs.

Mineral oil (sold by the quart as cutting board oil) is all you need. If you want to lubricate with motor oil, get the synthetic stuff, natural motor oil has a bad smell. One quart of synthetic oil will last a lifetime.

OP, there are major differences in oils. 3 in 1 oil is not suitable for guns, too thick. Actual "gun oil" however is light machine oil and very thin so it will get in-between parts where it is needed. However, some gun oil may not be suitable if you are in a cold climate. It may thicken enough that a semi-auto won't cycle reliably. Also, regular gun oil is just than, an oil only. The gun must be cleaned first with a powder solvent like Hoppes #9. A good alternative to both is BreakFree CLP (cleans, lubes, protects) or similar product. I've used it for years and you don't need much to do the job. It used to be what the military used although I read somewhere that Pro-7 LPX is also being used now. As far as I can tell the main difference is a bigger temp range (from -65F to -85F).

There used to be a rhyme for good gun practice, "Never let the sun set on a dirty gun.". This was true in the black powder era and also true if you are shooting corrosive military surplus. If you blow 50 rounds of Blazer at the range however it isn't going to ruin anything if you don't clean it right away. Also, if you use a CLP-type product for cleaning then the gun will be properly oiled from that, you don't need to do anything extra. Strip it, spray it, brush & patch the bore, and scrub the action with a brush, then wipe off all the excess, and reassemble.

You will be good to go.

More info here: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MIL-L-63460

I’m not a pro either, but I have many guns. All I can say is if you ask a question, you will get ten answers, all probably good. Keep it simple would be my suggestion. Anything that cleans and lubes will be fine. Hoppes, Rem oil, etc. once in a while I use a spray cleaner, then lube up. Brushes in the bore to scrape out lead deposits, etc. the biggest problem I have faced is storage corrosion/rust. It happened once. I moved my safe indoors after that, and now own three safes. Each has a heater and a dehumidifier that plugs in to recharge. Keep your shit dry and lubed.
